summary.text: 肉 is a whole-graph pictograph of a piece of meat or animal flesh; its strokes are not separate components.

formation.text: Pictographic: the graph as a whole depicts meat. The received Shuowen gloss is 胾肉, interpreted in a later annotation as a large piece of animal meat; this dictionary account does not establish the graph’s date or earliest use.

components.text: The whole graph 肉 depicts a piece of meat or animal flesh. Treat it as one picture rather than splitting its strokes into modern lookalikes.

history.text: 肉 is represented in oracle-bone, Chu manuscript, and Small Seal categories. The selected glyph is a modern drawing in Shuowen seal-script style, not an ancient specimen. Available descriptions do not date individual examples or establish a detailed sequence of graphic changes.
The graph’s pictographic explanation does not determine the deeper history of the spoken word. Proposed accounts of the word’s origin remain unresolved in the available research.

uncertainties.text: The available material does not establish the earliest attested use of the character’s senses, a complete sequence of graphic changes, or the deeper etymology of the spoken word.

senses.text: The received Shuowen account glosses 肉 as 胾肉, interpreted in its later annotation as a large piece of animal meat. Dictionary citations document uses for meat and bodily flesh but do not establish their exact dates or which use came first.
A dictionary records 肉 for fruit pulp, with a citation from 齊民要術. The date and any development from the meat sense are unresolved.

senses.gloss: solid part of a perforated ring
senses.text: Dictionary explanations and citations record 肉 for the solid part of a perforated ring. They do not establish when this use arose or how it relates to the meat sense.
A dictionary records a use of 肉 for musical voice or timbre. Its date and any semantic path from the meat sense are unresolved.
In current Chinese, 肉 means meat or flesh; the supplied record gives the Mandarin reading ròu.

limitations.text: Dictionary citations do not establish the earliest attestation of these senses or their chronological and semantic relationships, so no development is asserted without a dated sequence.
The pictographic account concerns the graph and its depicted referent; it does not resolve the spoken word’s deeper etymology. Proposed comparisons remain unresolved.
